title: Examples of Energy Transformation and Conservation of Energy
summary: Tracing the energy path in six devices, the principle of conservation of energy, and the dropped ball and pendulum demonstrations.

p: Study the table.

head: Device
Energy path
rows: Potential (water high up) → kinetic (falling water) → mechanical (turbine) → electrical

sections.h: The principle of conservation of energy
p: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only change from one form to another. The total energy stays the same. When you use a torch, the chemical energy in the battery is not gone; it has turned into an equal total of light and heat.

A ball held high has potential energy because of its height. When it is dropped, it loses height (potential energy goes down) and gains speed (kinetic energy goes up). Just before it hits the ground, almost all the potential energy has become kinetic energy (a little goes to air resistance as heat).

Pull the bob to one side (position A): it has maximum potential energy. Release it: at the bottom (position B) its energy is mostly kinetic and it moves fastest. At the other side (position C) it stops for a moment and the energy is potential again. The pendulum changes energy between potential and kinetic again and again, but slowly comes to rest because some energy goes to heat through friction with the air and the pivot.

(a) A car engine burning petrol: chemical → heat → mechanical (movement), with sound and heat wasted. (b) A solar-powered calculator: light → electrical → light (the display) and a little heat. (c) A person shouting: chemical (food) → mechanical (muscles) → sound. (d) A windmill making electricity: kinetic (wind) → mechanical (turning blades) → electrical.

A bouncing ball does not return to its starting height because on each bounce some of its energy is changed to heat and sound, so there is less energy left to lift it. Energy is not lost from the universe; it is spread into the surroundings.

title: Heat and Heat Transfer: Conduction and Convection
summary: What heat is, why it flows from hot to cold, and how it moves through solids by conduction and through liquids and gases by convection.

p: Heat (thermal energy) is energy that passes from a hotter object to a colder object. It is linked to the energy of motion of the particles in a substance: the hotter the substance, the faster its particles move or vibrate. Heat always flows from hot to cold, never the other way by itself.

Conduction is the transfer of heat through a substance by direct contact, from particle to particle, without the particles themselves moving from their places. They vibrate and pass the energy along. It happens mainly in solids. Example 1: the handle of a metal spoon in hot tea gets hot. Example 2: frying an egg: heat conducts from the stove to the pan and from the pan to the egg.

Convection is the transfer of heat through liquids and gases by the movement of the fluid itself. How a convection current forms: 1. The fluid at the bottom is heated. 2. It expands and becomes less dense (lighter). 3. The hot, light fluid rises. 4. The colder, denser fluid at the top sinks to take its place. 5. This is heated in turn and the cycle goes on.

Examples: water boiling in a pot; and the sea breeze. In the day the land heats faster than the sea, so the warm air over the land rises and cool air from the sea moves in to take its place. At night the land cools faster, and the breeze blows from land to sea (a land breeze).

sections.h: Why conduction in solids and convection in fluids?
p: In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and cannot move about, so they can only pass energy by vibrating against each other. In liquids and gases the particles are free to move, so the hot particles themselves can carry the heat from one place to another.

title: Radiation, Conductors, Insulators and the Vacuum Flask
summary: How heat travels as infrared waves, which materials conduct or insulate heat, and how a vacuum flask stops all three kinds of heat transfer.

p: Radiation is the transfer of heat as electromagnetic waves, mostly infrared. It needs no medium: it can travel through a vacuum. Examples: heat from the Sun reaching the Earth across millions of kilometres of empty space; feeling the heat of a bonfire from a distance even though the air between you and the fire is not moving. Dark, rough surfaces absorb and give out radiation well; shiny surfaces reflect it.
Study the table.

Conductors let heat pass easily: all metals such as silver, copper, aluminium and iron. That is why cooking pots are made of metal. Insulators do not let heat pass easily: wood, plastic, glass, rubber, cloth and air (trapped air is a very good insulator). That is why pot handles are plastic or wood, and why we wear thick, fluffy clothes in cold weather: they trap air.

A vacuum (thermos) flask keeps hot things hot and cold things cold by stopping all three kinds of heat transfer. It has two walls, like a bottle inside a bottle. Conduction is reduced because the stopper is plastic (an insulator) and the two walls touch only at the neck. Convection is stopped because there is a vacuum between the walls: no air, so no moving fluid. Radiation is reduced because the walls are coated with a shiny silver layer that reflects the heat back.

sections.h: A note on the microwave oven
p: The lesson note lists a microwave oven as an example of radiation. A microwave oven does use radiation (microwaves), but it works differently from heat radiation from the Sun: microwaves make the water molecules in food vibrate, and that heats the food from inside.

title: Electrical Energy: Sources, Current and Circuits
summary: What electrical energy and current are, the sources of electricity, and how a simple circuit is made and drawn with standard symbols.

p: Electrical energy is energy from the movement of electric charges, usually electrons. Electric current is the flow of charge through a conductor. It is measured in amperes (A).

Cells and batteries: chemical reactions push electrons through a wire (remote controls, phones, cars). Generators: a turbine turned by water, wind or steam from burning gas spins a magnet near coils of wire, which makes electrons move; this is how most large-scale power is made. Solar panels (photovoltaic cells): turn light directly into electricity. Others: wind turbines, hydropower dams and nuclear power stations. In Nigeria most grid electricity comes from gas-fired power stations and hydropower dams such as Kainji, Jebba and Shiroro; many homes also use solar panels and generators.
An electric circuit is a complete closed path in which current can flow. If the path is broken, for example by a cut wire or an open switch, it is an open circuit and the current stops.

title: Series and Parallel Circuits, Home Wiring and Saving Electricity
summary: The two ways of joining bulbs, why homes use parallel wiring, the live, neutral and earth wires, safety rules and ways to save electricity.

p: Study the table.

head: Feature
Series
Parallel
rows: Simple circuits, some old fairy lights

sections.h: Why homes are wired in parallel
p: If your lights were in series, one blown bulb would put out every light in the house, and each bulb would be dim. In parallel, each appliance gets the full voltage and can be switched on and off by itself.

The live wire (brown) carries the high voltage to the appliance. The neutral wire (blue) completes the circuit by carrying current back. The earth wire (green and yellow stripes) is a safety wire joined to the metal case of an appliance and to the ground. If the live wire touches the case, current goes safely to earth, the fuse blows, and you are not shocked. A fuse is a thin wire that melts if the current is too high and breaks the circuit.

1. Never touch switches, sockets or appliances with wet hands. 2. Do not overload a socket with too many powerful appliances, because it can start a fire. 3. Do not use appliances with frayed or broken wires. 4. Never poke metal objects or fingers into a socket. 5. Switch an appliance off before unplugging it. 6. Do not fly kites near overhead power lines. Never touch a fallen electric wire; call the power company.

Turn off lights and fans when you leave a room. Use energy-saving LED bulbs instead of old filament bulbs. Unplug TVs and chargers when not in use. Make sure the refrigerator door seals tightly. Saving electricity saves money and burns less fuel.

title: Science, Technology and National Development
summary: The meanings of science, technology and national development, and how they feed one another in a loop.

p: Science is a systematic way of getting knowledge about the natural world by observing, forming a hypothesis and experimenting. It asks 'why'. Technology is the use of scientific knowledge for practical purposes, the making of tools, machines and methods to solve problems. It asks 'how'. National development is the overall improvement of the quality of life and standard of living of the citizens of a country: a stronger economy, health care, education, roads, electricity and security.

img.alt: Three connected gears labelled Science (knowledge and research), Technology (application and tools) and National Development (progress and economy)
img.cap: Science, technology and national development drive one another.

p: 1. Science gives new knowledge and ideas. 2. Technology uses these ideas to make tools and solutions. 3. Development: these tools improve society, for example better medicine and faster communication. 4. A richer, better-educated country can pay for more science (universities and laboratories), which gives more knowledge, and the loop continues.

Example: Science: biologists found that the mould Penicillium kills bacteria. Technology: chemists and engineers learnt to produce penicillin in large amounts. Development: penicillin cures infections, saves millions of lives and improves national health.
The next picture shows the same message: science and technology hold the key to a nation's progress and quality of life.

title: Research, Contributions of Science and Technology, and Great Innovators
summary: Why research and development matters, how science and technology help farming, medicine, communication and industry, and the difference between a discovery, an invention and an innovation.

p: Research is the engine of science: finding out new knowledge. Development is the engine of technology: turning knowledge into products and methods. A country that spends a lot on R&D in universities and research institutes finds new solutions and makes new products, so it develops faster. The USA, China and South Korea are leaders in technology partly because they spend large amounts on R&D.
Study the table.

head: Sector

rows: Tractors, fertilisers, improved seeds and irrigation raise food production and food security
Understanding of disease plus vaccines, scanners and new drugs lead to longer, healthier lives

p: A discovery is finding something that already exists in nature, such as Isaac Newton's work on gravity. An invention is making something new that did not exist before, such as Thomas Edison's practical electric light bulb. An innovation is taking an existing invention and improving it a great deal or finding a new use for it.

International: Thomas Edison (light bulb, phonograph); Alexander Graham Bell (telephone); Tim Berners-Lee (invented the World Wide Web, which runs on the Internet; he did not invent the Internet itself). Nigerian: Jelani Aliyu, a Nigerian-born car designer who led the design of the first Chevrolet Volt, a plug-in electric car with a petrol range extender (a hybrid, not a fully electric car as some say); Prof. Wole Soboyejo, a materials scientist. There are many local innovators who build machines for garri processing and palm oil extraction, and engineers and young people who develop apps and solar products.
